title: Back to School: Three Big Challenges
gist: In a RAND Policy Minded podcast interview, Heather Schwartz of RAND Education, Employment, and Infrastructure presents survey data from RAND's 28,000-teacher panel and youth panels showing AI use in K-12 schools has roughly doubled in two years even as two-thirds of students say AI harms critical thinking, cell phone bans are now near-universal and measurably reduce in-class phone use, and chronic absenteeism has fallen from its pandemic peak but remains at 18 percent (about 10.8 million students), still above the 15 percent pre-pandemic baseline.

insights.claim: About half of K-12 public school teachers nationally are now using AI tools in their work, roughly double the rate of two years earlier, based on RAND's standing panel of about 28,000 public school teachers.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: A doubling of AI adoption among teachers in two years signals a fast-scaling addressable market for edtech and general-purpose AI vendors serving the K-12 sector.
insights.quote: about half of K–12 public school teachers are now using AI tools in their work. That's about double the rate from two years ago.
insights.locator: the headline here is that about half

insights.claim: AI use among teachers rises with the age of students taught: about two in ten elementary teachers use AI weekly, versus three in ten middle school teachers and four in ten high school teachers, as of spring 2026.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete adoption curve by grade band useful for targeting edtech products and forecasting near-term growth in high-school-focused AI tools.
insights.locator: So about two in 10 elementary teachers

insights.claim: Teachers mainly use AI to tailor materials to students' needs and create instructional content, such as adjusting reading passages to different reading levels or generating quiz questions and worksheets.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Identifies content-differentiation and worksheet/quiz generation as the leading current use cases, indicating where near-term edtech demand is concentrated.
insights.locator: mainly using AI to tailor their materials

insights.claim: Teachers and principals overwhelmingly use general-purpose AI tools like ChatGPT rather than education-specific tools such as Magic School, a pattern Schwartz describes, crediting Rebecca Winthrop, as 'shallow and wide' rather than 'narrow and deep' use.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: General-purpose chatbots are currently capturing the K-12 market ahead of purpose-built education AI vendors, a competitive-dynamics signal for edtech investors evaluating Magic School-type startups against OpenAI/ChatGPT.
insights.locator: far and away, teachers and principals are using general purpose tools

insights.claim: About two-thirds of middle schoolers and older students said they used AI for homework as of the last school year, up from about 50 percent two school years earlier, and most use it across three or more classes rather than a single subject.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Rapid, broad-based student AI adoption across subjects (not just math or writing) points to a large and growing usage base for general-purpose AI products among students.
insights.locator: about two-thirds of middle schoolers on up

insights.claim: Students report using AI mainly for 'study buddy' purposes: getting clearer explanations of assignments, brainstorming ideas, looking up facts, and drafting or revising writing.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Clarifies the dominant student use case as tutoring/explanation and writing support, relevant to product design and policy debates over academic integrity.
insights.locator: basically like "study buddy" help

insights.claim: Two-thirds of students agreed that the more you use AI, the more it harms critical thinking, up from about 50 percent two school years earlier, with the strongly-agree share also rising among middle schoolers, high schoolers, and college-age students.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: A majority of students self-report cognitive harm from AI use even as usage rises — a reputational and regulatory risk signal for AI companies and a demand driver for guardrail/verification tooling in edtech.
insights.quote: two-thirds of students agreed with the statement that the more you use AI, the more it harms critical thinking
insights.locator: the single most disturbing trend that I've been seeing

insights.claim: As of spring 2026, 80 percent of school principals reported their school or district has an AI policy or guidance, twice the share from two years earlier, but many teachers say the policy is absent or confusing.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: A gap between principal-reported policy existence and teacher-experienced clarity indicates weak implementation — an opening for compliance/policy-communication tools targeting districts.
insights.locator: 80 percent of school principals nationally told us

insights.claim: Current school AI guidance is mostly teacher-facing (explaining what AI is, training on lesson planning) rather than student-facing, and many districts rely on generic 'fair use'/no-plagiarism policies as their main AI guardrail.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Districts are under-governing student AI use relative to teacher use, a gap that vendors of student-facing AI compliance/monitoring tools could address.
insights.locator: The kinds of guidance and training

insights.claim: Illinois published an unusually extensive statewide AI guidance package requiring formal tool approval, data-privacy safeguards, clear disclosure, opt-out options, and human oversight — a high bar Schwartz says most schools have not yet reached.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Illinois's framework could become a template that other states copy, creating a compliance market for districts nationwide as more states follow suit.
insights.locator: Illinois just published a really extensive set

insights.claim: Schwartz believes students and teachers are primarily accessing AI through free chatbot accounts tied to personal or school-issued email addresses, calling the current environment 'wild west' with little enforceable structure.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Unmanaged, unlicensed AI access at scale in schools creates data-privacy exposure and undermines the enforceability of new state policies like Illinois's.
insights.quote: I think it's sort of wild west right now about how and what people are using AI for in schools.
insights.locator: My sense is that

insights.claim: Schwartz argues schools need to shift from a 'pull' model of AI (users querying a standalone chatbot, which risks doing the work for them) to a 'push' model where AI is embedded directly within curriculum and day-to-day instructional materials.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Frames the next wave of edtech opportunity as embedded, curriculum-integrated AI rather than standalone chatbots — a specific product-category thesis for investors.
insights.locator: schools need to move from this sort of push versus pull

insights.claim: Schwartz cites a specific use case she is excited about: AI analyzing real-time student answer data in a math class to flag patterns (e.g., four of ten students making a specific error) so the teacher can address the misconception directly.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: A concrete, teacher-endorsed embedded-AI use case (real-time formative-assessment analytics) that maps to an identifiable edtech product category.
insights.locator: if I'm a math teacher

insights.claim: Schwartz warns it is a mistake to let AI serve as a brainstorming crutch for students' 'first-draft thinking,' since that early recall-and-synthesis work is a necessary building block of learning that AI should not replace.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Articulates a pedagogical red line (AI should teach, not tell) that is likely to inform future state and district AI policy design.
insights.quote: AI that teaches, not tells, to use someone else's phrase.
insights.locator: Yeah, exactly. AI that teaches

insights.claim: About 90 percent of U.S. teens own a cell phone, and more than three-quarters of teachers and principals say phones are a major classroom distraction that harms classroom culture and school climate.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Near-universal phone ownership combined with strong educator consensus on harm explains the political momentum behind bell-to-bell ban legislation nationwide.
insights.locator: About 90 percent of U.S. teens have one

insights.claim: As of the last school year, about half of middle and high school students attended a school with a bell-to-bell cell phone ban, about a quarter attended schools banning phones only during class time, and the remaining quarter had schools with in-class use allowed or no ban at all.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Quantifies the current policy landscape, showing bell-to-bell bans have become the plurality approach — useful baseline for tracking further state-level mandate adoption.
insights.locator: about half of middle and high school students

insights.claim: Stricter phone policies measurably reduce in-class phone use: about 50 percent of students under bell-to-bell bans still checked their phone at least once daily in class, versus 80 percent of students in schools with looser restrictions.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Provides an evidence-based effect size for ban strictness on behavior, useful for districts and policymakers weighing the marginal benefit of stricter rules.
insights.locator: The good news here is that we do see

insights.claim: About half of students admit to evading school phone rules, such as hiding phones in pockets or using smartwatches as workarounds, but enforcement matters: only 17 percent of students with 'very strict' teachers hid phones, versus half of students with teachers who were 'only a little strict.'
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Shows enforcement consistency, not policy text alone, drives outcomes — a design implication for any technology or process aimed at supporting classroom compliance.
insights.locator: only 17 percent of students with teachers

insights.claim: 86 percent of principals said they favor cell phone restrictions, citing benefits to school safety, learning environment, and reduced distractions, and students report similar views on reduced distraction and improved school climate.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Broad stakeholder buy-in (both administrators and students) reduces political risk for districts adopting stricter bans, supporting continued policy diffusion.
insights.locator: 86 percent of principals said they're in favor

insights.claim: Schwartz does not expect cell phone bans alone to be a 'silver bullet' for improving math and reading achievement in the short run, viewing their clearest near-term payoff as improved school climate and reduced distraction rather than test-score gains.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations for near-term academic-outcome gains from phone-ban policy, which matters for how districts and researchers should frame success metrics.
insights.quote: I don't think school bans are going to be a silver bullet to improve math and reading achievement, at least not in the short run.
insights.locator: I think that schools should be realistic

insights.claim: Schwartz reports early evidence linking sustained cell phone bans to improvements in school absenteeism, a metric she describes as very hard to move, provided enforcement remains consistent over time.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: A previously undocumented secondary benefit — phone bans potentially reducing absenteeism — links two of the episode's major themes and could strengthen the policy case for districts.
insights.locator: I also think that schools should really be sticking

insights.claim: RAND's latest estimates show 18 percent of public school students were chronically absent (missing at least 10 percent of the school year, or 18-plus days) in the school year that ended a few months before this August 2026 interview, roughly 10.8 million students.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: A precise, current national absenteeism figure (18 percent, 10.8 million students) is a key input for forecasting learning-recovery timelines and related state education funding decisions.
insights.locator: we just published new estimates showing

insights.claim: Pre-pandemic chronic absenteeism was about 15 percent of students; it roughly doubled to about 30 percent in the 2021-22 school year at the pandemic peak, and has since declined to 18 percent but remains above the pre-pandemic baseline.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Establishes the full recovery trajectory (15 percent to 30 percent to 18 percent), showing meaningful but incomplete normalization four-plus years after the pandemic peak.
insights.locator: Pre-pandemic, it was about 15 percent

insights.claim: About half of large urban school districts had 30 percent or more of their students chronically absent as of one or two years ago, making urban districts the hardest hit by the absenteeism problem.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Identifies urban districts as the geographic concentration of absenteeism risk, relevant for targeting municipal bond, real estate, or public-service investment analysis tied to school quality.
insights.locator: Urban districts are hit hardest

insights.claim: Illness remains the most common reason students give for missing school, but mental health is a significant secondary factor, with many students reporting they take unofficial mental health days, alongside everyday causes like oversleeping or simply not wanting to go.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Confirms mental health as a material, quantifiable driver of absenteeism, supporting the case for school-based mental-health investment as an absenteeism intervention.
insights.locator: illness was still the most common reason

insights.claim: Schwartz attributes persistent post-pandemic absenteeism partly to an attitudinal shift toward greater tolerance of missing school for reasons like minor illness or feeling down, a norm shift that has proven hard for schools to reverse.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Identifies a durable behavioral/cultural driver of absenteeism (versus a purely logistical one), implying interventions must address parent and student norms, not just school operations.
insights.locator: there's been an attitudinal shift with COVID

insights.claim: The most common district strategies against absenteeism are early-warning outreach — calls, texts, or home visits before a student crosses the 15-to-18-day chronic threshold — and hiring dedicated attendance coordinators, though districts report these strategies have had only modest effectiveness.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Signals limited effectiveness of current district-level interventions, indicating an unsolved problem space where new approaches (e.g., community partnerships) could gain traction.
insights.locator: the most obvious thing that is important

insights.claim: Smaller and rural districts have less capacity than large districts to fund dedicated attendance-coordinator staff, creating uneven ability to run early-intervention programs.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Highlights a resource gap between large and small/rural districts in absenteeism response capacity, relevant to equity-focused education funding allocation.
insights.locator: Obviously larger districts have more capacity

insights.claim: Remote/online learning options during school interruptions (using school-issued devices like Chromebooks) remain in use post-COVID but appear to be declining and are viewed as an inferior substitute for in-person schooling.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Suggests declining reliance on remote-learning fallback options, a relevant signal for edtech companies that built products around pandemic-era remote instruction.
insights.locator: my impression from various things that I've been reading

insights.claim: Schwartz identifies a growing focus on high-quality, evidence-based instructional materials in math and reading as an optimistic trend, noting increasing alignment across the decentralized U.S. school system on these basics.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Signals rising demand and district willingness to adopt standardized, evidence-based curriculum products, a positive indicator for curriculum publishers with strong efficacy data.
insights.locator: Another trend that I'm seeing that I find optimistic

insights.claim: Schwartz notes schools face 'stiff headwinds' from funding cuts and enrollment drops that are causing some schools to shrink or consolidate, compounding the challenges posed by AI, cell phones, and absenteeism.
insights.speaker: Heather Schwartz
insights.so_what: Financial and demographic pressure on public school systems is a macro headwind relevant to municipal finance and education-sector investment, independent of the AI/phone/absenteeism trends discussed.
insights.locator: there's funding cuts, there's enrollment drops
